doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Where are the young black players; jazz education and universities
summary: Rowe notes jazz parties are elderly and white; Harris says black universities neglect jazz, listing New Orleans schools and their programs.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I’ve seen a similar thing with the jazz parties across the country that these promoters, different from festivals, you know they do these jazz parties where people come and they stay for the weekends and they listen to what you would I guess call classic or mainstream jazz. The two things I’ve noticed is that first of all the audience is all elderly people, they’re almost all white, and the musicians are almost all white. And I’m wondering where are the young or middle-aged black musicians to play that music? I’m talking about playing standards you know.

Well I know but if you look in New York and New Orleans, Chicago, again we go back to those mainstream cities where the music is being perpetuated, kids are learning the music in schools, and so young people are playing that. When you go to the International Association of Jazz Educators now and you’re right in a sense because when you look at the ratio of African-Americans versus white kids you see more white kids playing that. But it’s the black universities for the most part are not supporting that. So here the music went, so it started in the nightclubs, right? Then it kind of went to the college campuses. So now the college campuses, the HBCU’s, aren’t doing anything with the schools, but the white schools are playing it. I mean when you look at New Orleans, the University of New Orleans has an excellent jazz education program. Even the Louis Armstrong Educational Foundation now funds a master’s program in jazz studies which is a full ride for seven young college students and they also do outreach in New Orleans Public Schools in jazz education. But Xavier University, which is a New Orleans university, doesn’t have a jazz program. The University of — SUNO — Southern University of New Orleans, where Kidd headed the jazz studies program, just discontinued it. Kidd just retired. Dillard University had an artist in residence there and did a little something in jazz education but there’s no real jazz curriculum there.
No. That was before Katrina. But Tulane University has one and so does Loyola. They are two white universities.
And Tulane has the wonderful archive also.
Yeah. Um hum. It does. The Hogan Jazz Archive.
Yeah. Well it’s interesting. Sometimes I think the things that drive universities to do certain things are not necessarily for the sake of the music or whatever. They come from other —
Endowments, yes, like who are we trying to keep happy here so to speak. Or what are the other people doing?
Right. But you know what that means is the African-American community, especially those fortunate people in the community, they’ve got to step up.
